content.title: About
content.content: Hummus is a spread made from cooked chickpeas, tahini, olive oil, lemon juice and spices. The commercial version is produced in large batches, packaged in portion‑size containers and maintains a consistent flavor and texture over a long shelf life.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Hummus has ancient roots in the Middle East, where it has been a staple snack for over a thousand years.
Commercial producers often use pasteurization and preservative additives to extend shelf life up to 12 months.
Tahini (sesame paste) gives hummus its characteristic nutty aroma and adds healthy fats.
In the United States hummus became popular in the 1990s, and by 2020 consumption had increased more than five‑fold.
In several countries hummus is considered a national dish and is served with pita, vegetables, or as a sauce for other meals.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Chickpeas, the main ingredient, contain about 20 % protein, making hummus a good protein source for vegetarians.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Hummus provides both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting healthy digestion and blood‑sugar regulation.

items.title: Beneficial monounsaturated fats
items.content: Olive oil and tahini supply monounsaturated fatty acids that are heart‑friendly.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Hummus is rich in vitamin B6, folate, iron, magnesium and potassium, which support energy metabolism and nerve function.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Thanks to its protein and fiber content, hummus raises blood glucose slowly.

items.title: Chickpea allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to legumes, including chickpeas, which can cause reactions from skin rash to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Commercial hummus often contains added salt; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Preservatives and additives
items.content: To achieve long shelf life, preservatives such as potassium sorbate may be used, which some consumers prefer to avoid.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Because of olive oil and tahini, hummus is relatively calorie‑dense; moderation is important for weight management.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Hummus can be enjoyed as a dip for vegetables, bread, crackers, used as a spread in sandwiches, added to salads, soups, or as a sauce for meat and fish. It can also be gently warmed in the microwave for a softer texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store an opened container of hummus in the refrigerator at 2‑4 °C, tightly sealed. Once opened, it is usually good for 5‑7 days. Keep it away from air and contaminated utensils to prevent spoilage.
